See more Published 08 June 2026 12:01pm BST In the run-up to the 2002 World Cup we all found out what a metatarsal is. David Beckham created a national frenzy after suffering a foot injury, pitting him in a race against time to be fit for the competition, with an X-ray of the damaged bone making it on to back – and front – pages.Heading into this World Cup we have learnt a new set of words, phrases and acronyms, including price-gouging, fake scarcity and ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement). Sadly, none of them has anything to do with football or even the physical well-being of the England captain.This will not only be the biggest World Cup – 104 matches in 16 cities involving 48 nations and across three vast and varied countries – but the most politicised. And certainly the most commercially driven. And that does not feel like a comfortable or correct combination.But what did we expect when Fifa awarded the tournament to Canada, Mexico but, primarily, the United States, where 78 matches – including the quarter-finals, semi-finals and final – will be hosted?After all, the US is the capitalist capital of the world – with the most developed entertainment market. The cost of live sport there has surged through ticket resale apps. Technology has certainly led to more aggressive pricing and it was instructive that Gianni Infantino, the Fifa president, referred to each World Cup fixture as a “Super Bowl”. It patently is not and never should be. Infantino has referred to each World Cup fixture as a ‘Super Bowl’ Credit: Sam Hodde/Getty Images That one-off NFL contest generates more than $1.25bn (£940m) in revenue. The average price to watch it live has soared from $700 (£525) in 2006 to $10,000 (£7,500) this year. Infantino has taken a similar approach to pricing at the World Cup. He wants every match to be a money-spinning event in its own right and a game of football second. He has lost sight of what the tournament represents.Ally the US attitude to Fifa’s own exploitative mammon-driven approach and it is a distasteful, expensive cocktail where the fan, and the fan culture that has developed football into by far the most popular sport in the world, becomes nothing more than a cash machine (or ATM) trading on emotional blackmail. Infantino has breached the ethos of what the World Cup is about.During last summer’s Club World Cup, when there was the first (ignored) outcry over dynamic pricing – varying (usually increasing) prices based on real-time demands – Fifa even tried to hide behind an extraordinary claim that it could do nothing to prevent it as the governing body would be contravening US law.Now some of those US authorities – the attorneys general of New York and New Jersey – have blown a hole in that argument by launching an investigation into Fifa’s practices, subpoenaing the org
